IN LOOKING FOR EVIDENCE upon which to make statements about schizophrenia, psychiatrists routinely interview patients with a view to eliciting symptoms, complaints, reports of experience, evidence for "orientation" and the like. The point it is easy to forget is that all such interviewing is done by talking, and that all conclusions are therefore based upon verbal report, or upon the absence of an anticipated or expected verbal report. If a patient does not answer questions, we say, for example, that he is "withdrawn" or even that he has "regressed, " quite ignoring the fact that all such statements are interpretations of sentences made or not made in accordance with standard systems of expectation. In using language in this manner, we perform a series of operations somewhat similar in principle to that in which we use eyeglasses when we cannot otherwise see. We look through the glasses, ignoring them when they work all right. Similarly, when language yields a consensually satisfying result, we can ignore the myriad ways in which we know how frail a vessel language can be.

The basic shape of language-use is that of a reciprocity in which each statement complements the preceding one and leads on to a succeeding one. The pattern holds for a series of statements made by a single person or a series of statements made by a pair or a group of speakers. The expectation is that of a continuity from one such sentence to the next. When we do not find such a regularity, the tendency is to move to the interpretative stance and say, for example, that the series is characterized by "distractibility." This term, a noun, suggests strongly that distractibility exists, and it is possible then to set up elaborate investigations of distractibility, with discoveries of the "cause" and the "cure, " perhaps. IN 1960 HAROLD SEARLES pointed out the significance of the psychological importance of the nonhuman-environment as follows:

It is even more surprising that psychoanalytic theory has remained largely undeveloped in this important area when we consider the overwhelming abundance of data inherent in man's daily life, in our culture, indicating how essential to his psychological wellbeing is his relatedness to the nonhuman-environment (Searles, 1960, pp. 10–11).

By that time Donald Winnicott (1958) had already made his important contributions on the characteristics of the first beloved possession which he called a transitional object and which is part of that "third part of the life of a human being, a part we cannot ignore … an intermediate area of experiencing to which inner reality and external life contribute" (Winnicott, 1958).

The following essays were part of a panel presentation at the December 1976 meeting of The American Academy of Psychoanalysis. The panel, which dealt with the concepts of Donald Winnicott, as they pertain to child observation and its relevance to adult development and adult psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, was chaired by Dr. Leah Davidson.

IHAVE BEEN READING AND THINKING about the use of the self in the treatment situation for some time now. The question I want to address myself to has, I believe, important implications for the theory of technique in psychoanalysis. One way I can formulate this question is: What processes can give us the feeling that we know something about the patient and about ourselves?

I will first present a brief historical view of a body of writing dealing with the therapist's emotional reactions towards the patient. I will then address myself to the question I have posed, particularly as it affects the gathering of knowledge in the analytic process, approaching it from three points of view. First, I will present my view of countertransference and its use in treatment. Here the focus will be on the therapist's attitude toward his own feelings. Secondly, I will deal with the technical issue relating to anonymity and neutrality in structuring the analytic process, and their importance in facilitating analytic objectivity. It is my contention that without that structuring and objectivity, the indiscriminate use of countertransference material becomes reminiscent of the dangers of "wild analysis." Finally, I will discuss greed. Greed is a feeling with which we are all more or less familiar, and one which tends to be repressed because it is unacceptable in our culture. It will serve as an example of an emotional reaction that, when unconscious or repressed, may spark defenses which may interfere with the normal need to know in the analytic process.

DR. BIEBER REPORTS THAT HE has interviewed 1000 male homosexuals; he does not, however, describe his selection procedures. Nor does he describe socioeconomic characteristics, family histories, developmental histories, or sexual histories of these individuals. Dr. Bieber has every right to his opinion that "there is a causal relationship between parental influence and sexual object choice." Some clinicians and investigators would differ. If Dr. Bieber has material from 1000 interviews it should be published so that we can make distinctions between conclusions, hypotheses, and speculations.

In 1952, a Research Committee of the Society of Medical Psychoanalysts was formed (Bieber, 1962). Members of the Committee had 20 male homosexual patients in treatment who were utilized in a pilot study. A questionnaire was constructed and refined, and then three copies were distributed to each member of the Society of Medical Psychoanalysts together with a covering letter requesting each to fill out the questionnaire on every male homosexual presently in treatment.

The members were further requested to fill out additional questionnaires if they were treating more than three male homosexuals. In the event they were treating fewer than three or none, they were asked to fill out the unused questionnaires for heterosexual male patients. These heterosexual patients formed the comparison sample. No formal instruction for selection of the comparison cases was given.

Seventy-seven analysts participated in the study. Twenty-six contributed 47 homosexual patients and 55 comparisons. Thirty-two contributed the remaining homosexual cases and 19 contributed the remaining heterosexual cases.

WE ENGAGE REGULARLY IN A RITUAL of the most profound significance which is performed not only by academics and intellectuals but by the whole human race. We come together to reason with each other about relatively intractable subjects, to pursue radically different points of view and unpleasant connections regardless of our personal reactions to them. Our intercourse is governed by important though relatively unverbalized rules in much the same way that any interpersonal connection is. We have agreed to listen to each other carefully, to reject appeals to prejudice or rhetoric, to eschew as far as possible the mystical, the poorly defined, etc. The sweep of human history has taught us that not only is truth itself best served by these rules, but that the applications of truth, its engineering aspect, to human problems depend on them as well. Most important of all, we abhor violence: the laying on of hands or instruments in anger, or its incitement through words. We consider this totally destructive of any truth seeking enterprise. At the siege of Syracuse, while he was involved in a mathematical calculation, the great Archimedes was run through by a Roman soldier who would not wait till he finished his work (Durant, 1939). THE PURPOSE OF THIS PAPER is to discuss the contributions and limitations of biofeedback mechanisms in a case of hypertension. My presentation will focus on the role of cognition in mediating autonomic behavior in the laboratory and in psychotherapy. Since interpersonal dynamics are implicit in any therapeutic intervention, the importance of this aspect in biofeedback will be stressed. It is my view that where biofeedback research fails to consider cognitive, interpersonal, and attitudinal factors, its effectiveness is limited.

During the past two decades therapeutic techniques derived from learning theory (e.g., behavior modification therapy), have increased enormously. Research in biofeedback, as a special case of behavior modification, currently occupies a prominent position, thus adding autonomic responses to the list of behaviors that can be modified. The delay in the application of biofeedback techniques awaited the development of biomedical technology (Ezios, 1973). To modify essential hypertension, for example, a practical continuous monitoring device had to be designed to provide feedback at each heartbeat for variations in blood pressure.

"Biofeedback, " in the sense used in this paper, and in the current literature, is information derived from internal monitoring which is transmitted to an otherwise not physiologically utilizable sensory channel. Thus blood pressure variations can be "heard", or "seen." It was not until certain sophisticated electronic devices were developed that biofeedback could be a force in modifying behavior. How the person uses this information to modify his responses will be discussed here. In my view how the person uses the information has essentially to do with cognitive events (Ortof, 1973).

THE PRESENT REFLECTION ON THE CONNECTION between mythic belief systems and forms of psychopathology derives from the hypothesis of linguistic relativity which is generally associated with the names of Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf. The thesis

81

of linguistic relativity was stated more or less concisely by Sapir (1921) in the following terms:

Human beings do not live in the objective world alone, nor alone in the world of social activity as ordinarily understood, but are very much at the mercy of the particular language which has become the medium of expression for their society. It is quite an illusion to imagine that one adjusts to reality essentially without the use of language and the language is merely an incidental means of solving specific problems of communication or reflection. The fact of the matter is that the 'real world' is to a large extent unconsciously built up on the language habits of the group. … We see and hear and otherwise experience very largely as we do because the language habits of our community predispose certain choices of interpretation. (p. 134)

There can be little objection to my mind in basing one's approach to the problem of the relationship between patterns of psychopathology and the organization of mythic belief systems on the hypothesis of linguistic relativity. However, there are risks inherent in such an approach and the essence of my commentary is that the present essay has run those risks and has not avoided the implicit logical peril.

The risk inherent in this approach is that one mistakes the level of verbal behavior for the thought product that stands somehow behind, yet closely involved with and related to the patterns of verbal expression. If one reads, for example, Sapir's discussions of the relationships between language and thought, it becomes evident that the problem of language-thought connections cannot be simply reduced to considerations of verbal behavior. The problem is infinitely more complex. The argument of the present essay, however, seems to adopt an extreme position that infers thought content merely on the basis of verbal behavior and thus essentially distorts the Whorf—Sapir hypothesis. In so doing, the argument of the present essay obfuscates some of the more problematic and difficult considerations to which the organization of belief systems gives rise. I will try to return to this question in the latter part of the present discussion.

Ralph Slovenko  

DOES THE PSYCHOTHERAPIST TALK too much? Does the modern practice of psychotherapy threaten confidentiality? Whatever disagreement may exist regarding methods used by a therapist in the course of treatment, there is a near unanimity of opinion that nothing about a patient should be divulged to third parties. Allegedly, the patient's full participation, essential to psychotherapy, cannot be obtained without an assurance of absolute confidentiality.1

Central to a discussion on confidentiality is an examination of whether therapists are concealing what should be told and revealing what ought to be kept confidential. When may the therapist divulge, when should he divulge, and when must he divulge? Adopting the stance that he is protecting the patient's privacy and creating a "safe atmosphere" for all potential patients, it is possible that the therapist is concerned as well with his own privacy and his method of practice. At times it may be that the therapist's self-gratification, his self-esteem, prompts divulgences. These concerns of the therapist are legitimate, to be sure, but may do little to further the best interest or protection of the patient.

The traditional confidentiality between physician and patient is said to be threatened by the growing complexity of health care and the utilization of computers. The number of recent page-one

THE "SOFT" SOCIAL SCIENCES—psychology, sociology, history, etc. are in the need of development of critical standards analagous to the empirical standards of the physical sciences. When a physicist isolates one variable for study, develops a body of evidence and acquires an insight into the nature of physical reality, one desideratum is a replicable empirical test. Can he make predictions which can be duplicated by all observers? When Einstein theorized the constancy of the speed of light and the relativity of all other measurements, he predicted the bending of light in the neighborhood of the sun. The world became convinced when observation demonstrated that light does bend.

In the social and human sciences, flights of fancy are not only forgiveable, but need to be encouraged. The creative juices flow and new categories are invented and manipulated. Sometimes extraordinary insight is gained. Reality is so ambiguous and holistic that any system wrenched free can be easily criticized as reductionistic. This is a cheap shot. But social science is not a free-for-all either. There must be some standard of criticism.

Let me propose two standards: (1) A pragmatic standard; i.e., something can be understood better using the proposed set of abstractions; and (2) A poetic standard, i.e., this set of categories activates imagination instead of foreclosing it. By both of these standards John Murray Cuddihy's The Ordeal of Civility fails.

BOTH IN THE INITIAL PLENARY session and at the outset of the group discussion Dr. Levenson took the position that termination does not constitute much of a problem for him either technically or personally. Toward the close of the group session, Dr. Lippmann noted that Dr. Levenson's position seemed to have the effect on the discussion group of polarizing discussion. Group members were in

356

the position, much of the time, of trying to prove that termination was indeed a problem both personal and technical for the analyst, and issues of mourning and loss were emphasized.

Dr. Feinberg contrasted Dr. Levenson's views with Dr. Donald Meltzer's comments when he was visiting the Institute in the fall. Dr. Meltzer had described a cataclysmic life-death struggle at termination. Dr. Frankiel commented that one factor is that Dr. Meltzer treats many borderline patients, who tend to the dramatic intensity he describes. Dr. Davidson stated that this was perhaps also related to the cultural differences, and the characteristics of English child rearing.

Several seminar members noted that the end phase of an analysis is often ushered in by the thought, "If I work this out, the analysis has to end." Dr Lippmann pointed out that termination begins at the beginning of the analysis with the hope for a positive outcome.

Dr. Leiter observed, that termination is easy where the patient's goals and the analyst's goals are congruent. Patients often come to second analysts angry with the first since they were as Dr. Davidson put it, "Sold short on growth, " because the first analyst did not see the patient's full potential.

Most everyone agreed that there are some patients who are "missed" after they leave analysis, who have been specially important or meaningful to us, or patients we feel have "changed" us. Dr. Levenson denied "missing" terminated patients but did note that he was very pleased to see and hear about patients but did note that he was very pleased to see and hear about patients after they had left.

THE GROUP DEFINED ITS TASK as attempting to recount from personal experiences with termination, some of the issues we have met, with particular emphasis on how we would ideally like the process of analytic termination to go. We have all terminated analysis as analysands. Why look to our patients and to the literature for "issues" of termination, when we were once the "issue"? (Nachmani.) Theoretical and abstract issues were seen as secondary to our primary task of sharing our experiences with each other. The issue of an analytic relationship never having been adequately formed is not an infrequent factor involved in termination, in that analyst and analysand never get into a "good enough" trusting relationship. It is crucial that the patient forms an "attachment" to the analyst and vice versa in some way (Schecter), and without this underpinning of "authentic relatedness" (Feiner), a process misnamed "analysis" proceeds for years in so-called "attached" form until both quietly despair and bring up the issue of termination (Schecter).

There was agreement about the discontinuous nature of change and growth, and that analysis, as a change process, is also a discontinuous one. The terminal experience as a phase of analysis was seen as being as unique as the process itself. We emphasized the need to cover the same ground many times, and hence the need perhaps for a second analysis, to integrate what remains unfinished in the first. The post-analytic period was also seen as a time of going over old ground and integrating the experience of the analysis proper.

The group consensus about the process of termination focused on the necessity for confronting the patient with the reality of his life situation, and then leaving it to the patient to decide what he wanted to do. All agreed that the patient's subjective experience of termination should not be one of being "kicked out, " that such an experience may leave the patient with painful damage to his sense of self-esteem. (Szalita)

This horror of waking—this was knowledge. … He tried to fix it and hold it; he kept it there before him so that he might feel the pain. That, at least, belated and bitter had something of the taste of life.— Henry James, The Beast in the Jungle

NOT LONG AGO, A NEW PATIENT reported to me that he had seen the musical, "Jacques Brel is Alive and Well and Living in Paris", twenty-five times since the death of his wife, two years before. I had trouble understanding how anyone could sit through the same play so often, for any reason. Besides that, I wondered what could be making this man so morbidly attracted to words and music that were so bittersweet, cynical, and dysphoric. A few weeks later another patient described his fascination for Bette Middler. "I go to see her every chance I get and every single time I get depressed, but I love it. She represents something raw, primal, screaming, ranting, fuck-it-how-I-look. She magnifies her flaws; she's gut. I want to swallow her up and be her or at least be part of her life. She has power and pain; I want to share some of that." About the same time, still another patient described how a close friend told her something cruel and cutting. My patient was hurt but when the friend apologized the next day, she was vaguely disappointed. "I don't know why but I hate to have to surrender my bad feelings. Just because she was making up to me made me feel I no longer had the right to be upset." And still another patient described the following fantasy: "I wish there was a cause I felt really strong about. A fantasy I have over and over again is that I'm the last Jewish soldier between the Arabs and Tel Aviv and I know I'm going to die for a purpose. I have a smile on my face."

These little vignettes lend themselves to many different interpretations. Most striking, however, is the underlying thread of self-destructive, possibly masochistic attitudes.

PERPHAPS THE MOST USEFUL contribution I can make to the discussion of this interesting paper is to formulate the nature of the child's illness and the progress of his therapy from my particular vertex, hoping that it will be understood to imply no attempt to amplify or correct what is written. The method used, skillfully holding together in one therapist's hands the three roles of psychotherapist, manager of the hospital situation, and advisor to the parents, is very impressive but makes for some difficulty in following the transference events. So I will not attempt to do that but will only speak of Jimmy's psychological situation.

This child seems to me, in the wisdom of hindsight, to have broken down with a hypochondriacal psychosis (a variant of depressive illness, of the type manifest in Schreber's first breakdown) under the stress of an exploding family situation, the major factors being the sister's incipient paranoia, the parents marital difficulties and the prospective move which would take him away from the one object of love, Johnny. These impending disturbances impinged upon a personality which had achieved a false stability by means of severe splitting-and-idealization of self and objects. His malevolent self had been projected into his sister so that his tolerance of her persecution was based not on masochistic submission (her slave) but on guilt and sympathy for her (much as was the Wolf-man's relation to his sister, also later to be paranoid). Jimmy's omnipotence, increased by his parents' concurrence in his self-idealization, also was manifest in his guilt toward Patrick, whom he would have hated much as Mary had hated him, had he been born sound.

THE STRUGGLE OF MODERN WOMAN to disclaim cultural stereotypy and to claim her just and proper place in the social mainstream has only gained the intellectual stature it warrants in the past decade. Its entry into collective consciousness in our era, blatant with the exposé of social injustice and reckless suppression, while helping to identify personal and ideological enemies, has tended to obfuscate certain internal, psychological impediments to success.

In some women the realization of career objectives is elusive or mixed with anxiety and distress even in what appears to be a favorably inclined environment.1 Such women do and will occupy our clinical calendars and it is the purpose of this paper to discuss, first by examination of theory and then by case example, the pain, lameness, and too frequent failure that characterizes their efforts.

IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (Springmann, 1974 a) I suggested that application of Ezriel's concept of object relations, traditionally reserved for individual and small group analyses, could be useful in understanding and interpreting large group phenomena as well. I demonstrated, with the help of clinical examples, how patients in the large group could be helped as individuals, and as a whole group, to relinquish nonadaptive, pathological, defensive ("required") object relations, and replace them with so-called "avoided" relationships, more mature, reality oriented adaptive ones, which had hitherto to be avoided, because they had been causally connected in the patients' minds with imaginary calamitous results which would come into effect as soon as the avoided relationships became manifest.

I agreed with Ezriel and tried to demonstrate that this therapeutic result could be achieved by "complete interpretations, " which ought to spell out the current required relationship (by no means always consciously recognized and acknowledged as such), to reconstruct the avoided relationship and the imaginary calamity from hints contained in the material, or from any other available source. The therapist could point out and thus sever the causal connection between these last two relationships. I have come to refer to this kind of intervention, which contains all three layers of current object relations as "three level interpretation" (Springmann, 1974 b).

I then came across a sequence of two consecutive, dynamically interconnected large group sessions which demonstrated these points most unequivocally, after the paper on the subject (1974a) had been finished.

THE PRACTICE OF MULTIPLE ANALYSES, i.e., of seeing more than one analyst during an analysis, has long been an accepted pattern among Jungian analysts. This practice can further be broken down into (1) concurrent analyses, or (2) serial analyses. The major focus of this paper will be on concurrent analyses.

Historically, this practice began with Jung who often sent his patients to a woman colleague. Jung preferred to deal with the impersonal symbolic contents of the unconscious and would have the personal aspects dealt with by a woman colleague, (Wheelwright, 1975). Although multiple analyses has been a widely utilized practice, the literature on the subject is quite sparse. (Hillman, 1962) ; (Plaut, 1962) ; (Fordham, 1962) Furthermore, it is a practice which has given rise to a diversity of opinion among Jungian Training Institutes. It is the purpose of this paper to elucidate the theoretical basis for simultaneous multiple analyses, and to discuss the pros and cons of its practice. To do so, some basic concepts of analytical psychology related to multiple analyses will need to be defined.

Basic to analytical psychology is a dialectical method of conducting psychotherapy. The therapist abandons all of his preconceptions and techniques and confines himself to a purely dialectical procedure, not unlike Sullivan's conception of the analyst as a participant observer. The analyst "is equally a part of the psychic process of treatment and therefore, equally exposed to the transforming influences. (Jung, 1929) This "reciprocal reaction of two psychic systems" (Jung, 1935) represents a constant challenge to the analyst, which has to be met on the level of the patient. IN THE METROPOLITAN PRACTICE OF PSYCHOANALYTIC psychotherapy, we are on a familiar stage. The neurotic patient enters our setting, (when properly referred) more or less ready to consult with us, then to leave and carry on his life outside. We may think of the situation as primarily one between two individual actors, giving secondary attention to the group life of either.

When I went from training and practice in San Francisco, to practice with the Indian Health Service in Montana in 1971, I took with me this individual-patient-to-individual-therapist view of my work. My new role was principally one of consultant to mental health field staff who were located at small hospitals and clinics on the Montana and Wyoming reservations. I also had a small practice of Indian patients whom I could see once or twice a week.

What I could not ignore, after hearing scores of cases in consultation, was that most of the Indian patients came only once or twice. My own practice went better, but the relationships were tenuous. One common result could be said in several ways: Not much hope came from these meetings. The therapist was not idealized. The pairing bond between the patient and therapist tended to be very weak.

Actually, the clinical problems presented were not so different from urban practice as one might expect: anxiety over performance, depression after loss, loss of self-esteem from failure, and so forth. But whereas an empathic understanding of the therapist would draw forth increased gratitude and commitment from the patient in these settings I previously knew, this did not often happen here.

IN PRELITERATE CULTURES, human beings preoccupied with the marginal existence of the group celebrate reproductive activity and fertility in direct, symbolic fashion. In such cultures, phallic worship, the religious transformation of the reproductive state of the penis, is an overt manifestation of this crucial social concern. The phallus in this extension of meaning becomes a symbol not only for sexual excitement, but also for potency, in a sense implying successful competition for sexual partners. It is a relatively direct transformation of the territorial implications of the association of property and of access to females found again and again in modern ethological studies as associated conditions. Thus in the artifact, the phallus, there are the conjoint implications of potency in the sexual and in the aggressive senses.

The modern transformation in the significance of the phallus found in the complex literate civilizations, in which psychoanalysis has flourished, is well shown in two definitions of the term "ithyphallic, " sometimes found in museum descriptions. The prefix ithy- means "erect, " and the root phallos means "penis", so that ithyphallic is in modern context a tautology. The first definition given has to do with the religious symbolic images used in Bacchic rites. The second definition, dating from 1864, toward the middle of the Victorian era, is "grossly indecent." In between, as Freud points out, there lies the epoch giving rise to his aphorism that "civilization depends upon sexual repression." IT IS WITH GREAT PLEASURE that I offer my commentary on Dr. Friedman's paper Psychodynamics and Sexual Object Choice (Friedman, 1976).

At the outset I wish to seriously question the author's conclusion that "the patient has always been heterosexual." In my opinion he shows both homosexual and transvestitic conflicts but somehow has managed to function sexually with the opposite sex. This is a common phenomenon in those with sexual deviations. I AM PARTICULARLY GLAD that Kirsch should have made a coherent, informative and much needed statement on 'Multiple Analyses'. Heretofore only Hillman (1962) has published anything about it.

AUTHORS SEDERER AND SEIDENBERG address a difficult issue in attempting to spell out the influences of society on the ego ideal, and the ways in which the ego ideal, in turn, affects aspirations

251

in women. The major points in this paper have been verified by current research (Horner, 1972) ; (Dalsimer, 1975) and clinical evidence. Emphasis on the current struggle for work equality in political and social terms can obscure a particular woman's internal conflicts about success; achievement may be conflicted even in externally optimal situations; women, more often than men, fear and avoid achievement.

We also agree with the authors' implication that there may be a lag between the ideal self and the psychological wherewithal to actualize this ideal in one's own life. This discrepancy can exist between a woman's goals and behavior or between her behavior and her experience of self. Thus, an individual woman may be competent in her career, but she may or may not experience herself as equal to men. Even a professionally successful woman may not be able to dispel the sense that she is inferior.

In the course of developing their ideas, the authors make a number of points with which we disagree. In our view, many of the central issues relevant to the question of sex-role identification and achievement have been oversimplified. In setting down some of our thoughts on the matter, we were repeatedly impressed with the difficulty of determining how the expectations of society are integrated into the intrapsychic life of individuals. Drive strength, biological predispositions, life history, as well as social values bear on the problem.

1. In emphasizing the oppression which women have suffered, the authors seem to ignore the fact that both men and women are part of the same social system and that each operates out of expectations that are in some ways complementary. As the system changes, there will be new prerogatives and new demands for both sexes.

2. The authors make unwarranted assumptions about the gratification of work outside the home and the ungratifying nature of work inside the home.

THIS PAPER DOES NOT PRETEND TO BE a demonstration of anything. I have written as though talking with a colleague, making no attempt to feign delicacy or detachment. I know that our field is already overburdened with this sort of sincere, rough personal declaration. My excuse is the topic: Regarding the definition of our profession, I assume that you share a concern with me, and that it will lead you along the same paths it leads me, and that if it does not, then the point where you balk is the point where we can have a more careful and learned debate.

Defining psychotherapy, like any nonformal defining, is a methodological nightmare. We can cite all the examples we like, but ultimately we simply have to hope that, as discussants, we have the same thing in view. To begin with, then, I blithely assume that the strains and stresses of practice give us all a tacit, vague, common ground, on the basis of which explicit definitions of therapy can be debated. I am not interested in the sociology of practice, which would require a preliminary sketch of healing techniques. I am interested in an explication of what psychotherapists generally have in mind, or what would best get together the various things they have in mind, when they identify themselves as therapists.

A further warning: Please bear in mind throughout that I am not discussing or comparing techniques. When I refer to eclectic or single-minded formulas, I am not referring to eclectic or single-minded procedures. Eclectic therapists may have very simple and rigid definitions of therapy, and highly-programed therapists may have shopping-lists of rationales for their efficacy. I am sure that the way a therapist defines therapy does affect his practice and vice-versa, but it is no simple relationship, and I only allude to that relationship in passing.

THE PATIENT WHO DEVELOPS STUPOR and sleep during the analytic session has been a subject of interest to psychoanalytic investigators over many years. As early as 1914, Ferenzi (1950) recognized this condition as an important resistance problem. Freud, in the Metapsychological Supplement to the Theory of Dreams (1916) likened the withdrawal of interest which results in sleep to the womb-like, prenatal state, and wrote of two forms of temporal regression—primary narcissism and hallucinatory wish fulfillment. Later, in the General Introduction to Psychoanalysis of the Ego (1921), he drew attention to sleep as a way of avoiding the pain of reality brought to bear on the infant following birth.

Among those contributing in more recent times, Gabe (1951) has related the patient's sleep to a wish to be united with the good mother and to hallucinatory wish fulfillment. Lewin (1954), Parkin (1955), and Scott (1956) have stressed the importance of narcissistic elements and the blissful escape from external reality through sleep. Dousuzkov (1952) has made reference to hostile urethral impulses expressed against the analyst via sleep, and Stone (1947) has related the patient's sleep to a rivalrous, hostile refusal or inability on the part of the infant to nurse and receive from the breast. This latter paper expands our understanding in that the sleep in question is no longer considered to express only a regressive wish, i.e., for the good breast of mother, but draws attention to a form of hostility which expresses a rejection of and denial of the existence of a good object.

IN THIS PAPER, I discuss some unfortunately neglected aspects of the development of psychotherapeutic inquiry from hypnosis to early psychoanalysis. If we closely review those aspects from the vantage point of our current pluralism of perspectives on the inquiry and experience, they can throw new light on the distinction between the empirical and systematic psychology, on one hand, and the many different interpretive metapsychologies on the other. We may, thereby, strengthen the ground of the current foundation, and, also, clarify the possible, future direction for advances in our views of the relation between theory and practice.

There is little question about the original, therapeutic aims of hypnosis and of early psychoanalysis. For the main, original aims of those two procedures were, in fact, the same, i.e., first, from a dynamic, transformational point of view, to overcome the resistances caused by the unconscious repressions; and secondly, from a descriptive, observational point of view, to recover the lost memories interpreted to cause the pathological symptoms.

But those two procedures of psychotherapy fell under two, radically different sets of psychic conditions: that of hypnosis being constructed by means of directed inquiry into a trance state; and that of early psychoanalysis, by way of contrast, being constructed during the process of associative inquiry into a waking state.

THIS SUBJECT, TO WHICH I WAS ASKED TO address myself, highlights what I have thought of frequently and ruefully as my middle-age identity crisis. QUESTION OF TERMINATION belong to that large category of queries which are seldom made unless the questioner is already in trouble; i.e., it is not so much a question as a confession of difficulty. Ideally, termination is a natural extension of the totality and wholeness of the therapy; and, although it is true that the terms of termination might satisfy neither the therapist's nor the patient's idealizations, they should both have some intuitive feel for whether the termination is appropriate and harmonious.

The issue of termination may be approached as a problem in the therapist's aesthetics. There are some therapists who would agree with Valéry when he said of a poem, that it is never finished, it is only abandoned. There are others who take the opposite position: that every artist should have someone standing by with a mallet to hit him over the head when his painting is finished. In other words, therapy can be conceived of as having a definite end which should not be overextended; or, as having no end at all. There is an old saw that states that the therapy is finished when both therapist and patient know it is interminable. Lacan, on the other hand, has said that a therapy is finished when the patient knows what the therapist knows, which is what the patient already knew (Lacan, 1972).

I AM PLEASED TO HAVE THIS opportunity to respond to Dr. Schimel's critique of my paper because I believe discussions of this kind can only improve and enlarge upon our understanding. In this regard, however, it is somewhat regrettable that his doubt that the patient's psychodynamics were "sufficient to explain the phenomenon of patient's sleep" precluded his commenting on this aspect of my presentation, since it deprives me and the reader of the contribution he might have made in this area. On the other hand, his skepticism has rewarded us in another area, when he asks: "Is patient wakefulness an artifact induced by the psychoanalyst's countertransference?"

It will facilitate matters to summarize briefly certain aspects of my hypothesis. Patients who "sleep" in the psychoanalytic session operate with powerful denial of frustration, as well as infantile envy and jealousy, which renders them incapable of dealing in a satisfactory manner with the loss of the primary object. This denial operates via devaluating attacks on the breast (Klein) and on the mental apparatus (Bion). These latter attacks effect, in particular, analytic thinking and awareness of thoughts and feelings.

There thus develops a hatred of twoness and the linking function necessary to form a coherent whole. Aside from the splitting and scattering effect brought about by these attacks, what develops is a denial of self worth and object value, in favor of an omnipotent sense of superiority or megalomania. One of the significant manifestations arising from this hostility is the development of a kind of superficial concept of the world, in which real knowledge derived from any depth, including the unconscious, is denied.

What is particularly noted with such patients is their attempt to keep all explanations on a most superficial level, where emotions of unconscious origin are explained on the basis of present-day reality. In attempting to hide infantile anxiety in external reality in this manner, the patient will (unconsciously) try to seduce (or enlist) the analyst to collude with him.

ONE OF THE CHARACTERISTIC FEATURES of current times is a resurgence of interest in mysticism and religious movements. This interest coincides with an upsurge of violence, which, while publicly condemned, is enjoined and vicariously enjoyed by a large proportion of law-abiding citizens. I propose that such a coincidence is not accidental; that those attracted to mystical movements are likely to be individuals who, sensitized by the violence around them, become preoccupied with their own potential for violence, which they find too threatening to express and are unable to neutralize within the available family and societal context. This group is particularly disconcerting because it cannot be fit into any of the familiar categories, that is, diagnosed in conventional terms. I hope that my attempt here will not add to the present confusion. I ASSUME THAT THE PARTICIPANTS of the workshop perused the suggested reading which is quite representative of the various schools of thought. Included in the assigned reading is my paper, Reanalysis(Szalita, 1968) so I find it redundant to reiterate the criteria for termination and the problems it presents. I shall confine myself to a few thoughts I would like to share with this audience.

342

There are as many terminations as there are people who are being analyzed; and there are as many ways of getting analyzed. I think that there are also various ways in which each of us attempts to do analysis, particularly in those cases where the prerequisites for analyzability are not clearly present, which is often the case. To amplify briefly: analysis is a well defined method which has to be adapted to the capacity of each individual. While it is a truism to say that there are common features to all men and women in a given culture, there are also marked individual differences, to which we are often not sufficiently attuned.

It seems appropriate to omit from our present discussion all those situations when analysis is interrupted for whatever reason, in order to confine ourselves to termination proper. In those cases where analysis is indicated and proceeds in the way outlined by the technique, termination comes about in a more or less natural way. Both participants come to a conclusion that they have gone as far as they could, and both are satisfied with the results achieved. This does not happen very often, but each one of us has had such cases. We do not hear much from them or about them. They rarely get into the literature. Freud in his paper on "Analysis Terminable and Interminable", stressed, as we well remember, that the traumatic neuroses do yield such results.

Someone once said that we all analyze ourselves in others. In a sense this is very true. What is paid attention to, the inquiries made, the selection and emphasis are, perhaps, more related to our own experience and thoughts than is acknowledged. If one keeps this in mind, one is more tentative in the interventions and more attuned and open to differences in personality structure and life experience. We share our thoughts and leave it to the analysand to decide what is applicable to him.

THE PSYCHOANALYST IS SOMEWHAT like Racine who enclosed the irrationality of passions in a concise, chaste, rational dramatic form that reflects, for us, the measured harmony of Louis XIV's Versailles Gardens. This pattern of a rational presentation of the irrational created, for Racine's audiences, an intolerable tension relieved only by the final deaths, suicides, and painful enlightenments of his tragedies.

The psychoanalyst also attempts to define the irrational through a rational, fictive structure. When he succeeds, it is because the living organism has performed for him, and he is called upon to rearrange and interpret the vagaries, inconsistencies and contradictions in that performance. His problem is mainly one of language: to assemble from his particular experience sentences that are, or lead to, generalizations. The deeper semantic problem of determining what anyone means by anything he says, or says he does, further complicates his work. It would be easier if people thought and spoke mathematics.

When the psychoanalyst attempts to practice his craft of rearrangement and interpretation without the living organism before him, he is at a disadvantage. This is most evident in the criticism of literature, when he analyzes the impulses, drives, and preoccupations of dead writers by studying their works and words and the commentaries of their contemporaries. At the heart of the dilemma is an assumption that the family history, letters, notes, essays and diaries of the writer provide revealing insights into his neuroses and they, in turn, provide insight into the form and content of his work. The assumption is deceptive, and often leads to unsound critical conclusions. Once made, it generates a misleading double vision in which criticism becomes a psychoanalytical conclusion, and a piece of fiction is treated as though it were a man.

Language in its primitive forms ought to be regarded and studied against the background of human activities and as a mode of human behavior in practical matters. We have to realize that language originally, among primitive, noncivilized peoples was never used as a mere mirror of reflected thought. The manner in which I am using it now, in writing these words, the manner in which the author of a book, or a papyrus or a hewn inscription has to use it, is a very far-fetched and derivative function of language. In this, language becomes a condensed piece of reflection, a record of fact or thought. In its primitive uses, language functions as a link in concerted human activity, as a piece of human behavior. It is a mode of action and not an instrument of reflection.— Bronislav Malinowski(1923)

Allan Cooper Ph.D.

Allan Cooper

Allan Cooper, Ph.D.
220 Central Pk. South.

Allan Cooper  

THE MORNING WORKSHOPS TOUCHED on many issues. Opening the afternoon session I raised a question touched on in the literature and in some of the workshops. The comments that follow, are excerpted from the afternoon discussion. I asked if the terminal phase of analysis always included a period of mourning.

Not necessarily. (Szalita) For the analysts it is similar to having children leave home. (Gilbert) You have to differentiate between mourning and pathological mourning such as when there has been an early loss of the mother. (Moulton) Termination means something different to one's self, than it does to one's analyst, and may be different from the patient's reactions. (Szalita) Termination for people in this field is different from people not in the field. For the analyst it is important to understand what expectations he has of the analysand-in-training. The situation and circumstance of termination is important. What does it mean to terminate a training analysis with someone you still see once a month, or have dinner with before coming to a meeting? (Witenberg) The perception of the issue of mourning has much to do with one's value system. Some people feel that there has been more authenticity and sensitivity if the patient, and especially the analyst, mourns the termination. Maybe its okay to feel relief at the termination of an analysis. (Levenson) Often the pain of leaving is the pain of unrealized claims. (Mendelson) Sometimes a non-relationship has existed, and it is this, that is hard to face when stopping analysis. (Schecter) Where there is more ambivalence and trauma in childhood, stopping is more difficult. (Moulton) When I stopped my analysis I missed Paris, not my analyst. I was too busy working to miss my analyst. As a result of my analysis I did feel more independent, more grown-up, and more myself. (Szalita) I think you can leave analysis with both pleasure and regret. They are not mutually exclusive (Schecter). It's like reading a good book. I'm sad when its over, but I don't want to start it over again. (Szalita) People who have suffered a lot of pain have the defense of detachment. Sullivan called it somnolent detachment, and Bowlby called it the third stage of detachment. Everyone has it, and uses it as a defense. Patients use it as a defense against getting attached or over attached to the analyst (Schecter).

Severe Regression in an Eight-And-One-Half Year Old Boy

Ildiko Mohacsy M.D.

Ildiko Mohacsy

Ildiko Mohacsy, M.D.
68 East 86th Street
New York, New York 10028

Ildiko Mohacsy  

THIS PAPER DEMONSTRATES the rapid remission of the severe symptomatology of an eight and a half year old child, which can be attributed to intensive psychotherapy and to a special hospital environment in which each member of the staff took particular professional interest in the case. Due to their cooperation and understanding, the child's transference responses developed toward several nurses according to the changing phases of his therapy. Therefore the child had an opportunity to shift the emphases of his everchanging transference reactions from the figure of the therapist to other persons as well.

At the request of the parents I visited their son Jimmy, age eight and one-half, on the pediatric ward of one of New York's teaching hospitals. I found the child curled up, in a fetal position, in a wheelchair. Since he did not use his hands, the wheelchair had to be moved by the staff. He claimed that he could not walk and that he was blind. He soiled and wet himself and had to be spoon-fed by the nurses. His barking cough disturbed the whole ward. He groaned and moaned constantly and complained about his terrible pain in a whining voice. There were no abnormal neurological findings, and the tentative diagnosis was childhood psychosis.

The parents agreed to have him transferred, under my care, to the child psychiatry ward of the hospital. They gave the following history.

The patient was the middle child of upper-middle-class parents. His sister Mary, ten years his senior, hated him from the moment he was born. During his first year she dislocated his arm by twisting it.

I would like to express my extreme gratitude to Ann Turkel and Blanche Ross for their help during the preparation of this paper.

Transitional Phenomena in the Treatment of Adolescents

Muriel Straetz M.D.

Muriel Straetz

Muriel R. Straetz, M.D.
Department of Psychiatry and Human Behavior College of Medicine University of California, Irvine
Irvine, California 92717

Muriel Straetz  

I WOULD LIKE TO DRAW ATTENTION in these remarks to the rich possibilities that lie in the application of Winnicott's concepts on transitional objects and phenomena to some psychopathologic aspects of adolescent behavior and the problems of their treatment. At a time when the adolescent is in transition from dependency on family to membership in a wider social group as an individual responsible for himself, we may witness pathological manifestations involving the exaggerated or distorted use of transitional phenomena, whose function is to deny the threat of loss and separation.

In a previous presentation (Straetz, 1975), I offered a tentative hypothesis about the role of transitional phenomena in hysterical psychosis in ghetto adolescents facing separation and loss under conditions of long-term deprivation. There is now a small but growing literature on the integration of Winnicott's constructs with a variety of other clinical pictures in adolescence.
